question: In adults with type 2 diabetes or at cardiovascular risk in cardiovascular-outcome trials that include participants with and without baseline heart failure, do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hospitalization for heart failure versus placebo?

sources.text: Dapagliflozin and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes. BACKGROUND: The cardiovascular safety profile of dapagliflozin, a selective inhibitor of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 that promotes glucosuria in patients with type 2 diabetes, is undefined. METHODS: We randomly assigned patients with type 2 diabetes who had or were at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease to receive either dapagliflozin or placebo. The primary safety outcome was a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke. The primary efficacy outcomes were MACE and a composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure. Secondary efficacy outcomes were a renal composite (≥40% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate to <60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, new end-stage renal disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes) and death from any cause. RESULTS: We evaluated 17,160 patients, including 10,186 without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, who were followed for a median of 4.2 years. In the primary safety outcome analysis, dapagliflozin met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to placebo with respect to MACE (upper boundary of the 95% confidence interval [CI], <1.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). In the two primary efficacy analyses, dapagliflozin did not result in a lower rate of MACE (8.8% in the dapagliflozin group and 9.4% in the placebo group; hazard ratio, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.84 to 1.03; P=0.17) but did result in a lower rate of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure (4.9% vs. 5.8%; hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.73 to 0.95; P=0.005), which reflected a lower rate of hospitalization for heart failure (hazard ratio, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.61 to 0.88); there was no between-group difference in cardiovascular death (hazard ratio, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.82 to 1.17). A renal event occurred in 4.3% in the dapagliflozin group and in 5.6% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.87), and death from any cause occurred in 6.2% and 6.6%, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.82 to 1.04). Diabetic ketoacidosis was more common with dapagliflozin than with placebo (0.3% vs. 0.1%, P=0.02), as was the rate of genital infections that led to discontinuation of the regimen or that were considered to be serious adverse events (0.9% vs. 0.1%, P<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In patients with type 2 diabetes who had or were at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, treatment with dapagliflozin did not result in a higher or lower rate of MACE than placebo but did result in a lower rate of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, a finding that reflects a lower rate of hospitalization for heart failure. (Funded by AstraZeneca; DECLARE-TIMI 58 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT01730534 .).

Dapagliflozin and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes. Methods We randomly assigned patients with type 2 diabetes who had or were at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease to receive either dapagliflozin or placebo. The primary safety outcome was a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke. The primary efficacy outcomes were MACE and a composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure. Secondary efficacy outcomes were a renal composite (≥40% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate to <60 ml per minute per 1.73 m 2 of body-surface area, new end-stage renal disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes) and death from any cause. Results We evaluated 17,160 patients, including 10,186 without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, who were followed for a median of 4.2 years. In the primary safety outcome analysis, dapagliflozin met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to placebo with respect to MACE (upper boundary of the 95% confidence interval [CI], <1.3; P<0.001 for noninferiority). A renal event occurred in 4.3% in the dapagliflozin group and in 5.6% in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.87), and death from any cause occurred in 6.2% and 6.6%, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.82 to 1.04). Diabetic ketoacidosis was more common with dapagliflozin than with placebo (0.3% vs. 0.1%, P=0.02), as was the rate of genital infections that led to discontinuation of the regimen or that were considered to be serious adverse events (0.9% vs. 0.1%, P<0.001). Conclusions In patients with type 2 diabetes who had or were at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, treatment with dapagliflozin did not result in a higher or lower rate of MACE than placebo but did result in a lower rate of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, a finding that reflects a lower rate of hospitalization for heart failure. Effect of Dapagliflozin on Heart Failure and Mortality in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Background In DECLARE-TIMI 58 (Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events-Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 58), the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor dapagliflozin reduced the composite end point of cardiovascular death/hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) in a broad population of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. However, the impact of baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) on the clinical benefit of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition is unknown. Methods In the DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial, baseline heart failure (HF) status was collected from all patients, and EF was collected when available. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) was defined as EF <45%. Outcomes of interest were the composite of cardiovascular death/HHF, its components, and all-cause mortality. Results Of 17 160 patients, 671 (3.9%) had HFrEF, 1316 (7.7%) had HF without known reduced EF, and 15 173 (88.4%) had no history of HF at baseline. Dapagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death/HHF more in patients with HFrEF (hazard ratio [HR], 0.62 [95% CI, 0.45-0.86]) than in those without HFrEF (HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.76-1.02]; P for interaction=0.046), in whom the treatment effect of dapagliflozin was similar in those with HF without known reduced EF (HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.66-1.17]) and those without HF (HR, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.74-1.03]). Whereas dapagliflozin reduced HHF both in those with (HR, 0.64 [95% CI, 0.43-0.95]) and in those without HFrEF (HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.62-0.92]), it reduced cardiovascular death only in patients with HFrEF (HR, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.34-0.90]) but not in those without HFrEF (HR, 1.08 [95% CI, 0.89-1.31]; P for interaction=0.012). Likewise, dapagliflozin reduced all-cause mortality in patients with HFrEF (HR, 0.59 [95% CI, 0.40-0.88;) but not in those without HFrEF (HR, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.86-1.10]; P for interaction=0.016). Conclusions In the first sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor cardiovascular outcome trial to evaluate patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus stratified by EF, we found that dapagliflozin reduced HHF in patients with and without HFrEF and reduced cardiovascular death and all-cause mortality in patients with HFrEF. Abstract Background Galectin‐3 (Gal‐3) is a circulating biomarker of fibrosis, with higher levels being associated with an increased risk of progression of heart failure and kidney disease. Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are at increased risk of both. Methods DECLARE‐TIMI 58 was a randomized, placebo‐controlled trial of dapagliflozin in patients with T2DM with or at high risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and creatinine clearance ≥60 mL/min. In a nested biomarker substudy, Gal‐3 was measured at baseline and in adjusted analyses associated with the prespecified kidney‐specific composite endpoint [Kidney‐EP; sustained ≥40% decrease in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) to <60 mL/min, new end‐stage kidney disease or adjudicated kidney‐related death]. Results Among 14 530 pts, median Gal‐3 was 14.9 ng/mL [interquartile range (IQR), 11.9, 18.4]. Gal‐3 was weakly associated with urine albumin creatinine ratio ( r = 0.098, P < 0.0001) and eGFR ( r = −0.27, P < 0.001) at baseline and independently associated with the Kidney‐EP:adj hazard ratio (HR) 1.15 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03, 1.28] per 1‐SD log (Gal‐3), P = 0.013. Dapagliflozin significantly reduced the relative risk of the Kidney‐EP across quartiles of baseline Gal‐3 [overall HR 0.45 (95% CI 0.23, 0.85), P < 0.0001; P interaction = 0.87]. A greater risk difference was observed with dapagliflozin in patients with higher Gal‐3, in whom a higher absolute risk at baseline was observed [absolute risk reduction (ARR) Q4 1.9 (95% CI 0.6, 3.2) vs. Q1 0.6% (−0.1, 1.3), ARR P trend 0.048]. Conclusions Plasma Gal‐3 is independently associated with the progression of kidney dysfunction in patients with T2DM and normal kidney function. There was a gradient of greater absolute benefit for reducing kidney disease progression in patients treated with dapagliflozin and with higher Gal‐3 concentrations at baseline, in whom a higher absolute risk was observed. ESC Heart Failure , 12 : 3981 – 3986 . 10.1002/ehf2.15415 . PMC12719846 40952180 What is the clinical question being addressed? Is the biomarker galectin‐3 useful for risk assessment for kidney outcomes? What are the clinical implications? In patients with diabetes and without chronic kidney disease, galectin‐3 is associated with future kidney function decline. Dapagliflozin has great absolute risk reduction in patients with highest level. Introduction Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a major risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD). Galectin‐3, a member of the beta‐galactoside‐binding lectin family, plays important roles in multiple cellular processes, including cellular growth, differentiation and apoptosis. It has been studied as a cardiovascular biomarker in different settings and is implicated in fibrotic processes in various organs, including the kidney, with circulating levels providing an indicator of underlying organ fibrosis. Observational studies have shown an association between galectin‐3 and worsening kidney function in patients with established CKD and in the general population. , However, whether galectin‐3 can improve risk stratification beyond clinical factors or identify patients at actionable risk, as suggested by pre‐clinical data, remains uncertain. The sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 inhibitor dapagliflozin has been shown to reduce the risk of decline in kidney function and related outcomes. Hence, the aim of the present study was to investigate the association of galectin‐3 with worsening kidney function in patients at high risk (i.e., patients with T2DM) and assess the impact of dapagliflozin. Methods This nested biomarker sub‐study was conducted in the Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events (DECLARE)‐TIMI 58 trial, a double‐blind placebo‐controlled trial of dapagliflozin in patients with T2DM and a screening creatinine clearance >60 mL/min. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria have been reported. Blood plasma samples were collected at baseline using EDTA anticoagulant tubes and stored at −20°C or colder until shipped on dry ice to the central laboratory, where storage was at −70°C or colder until thawed for analyses conducted at the TIMI Clinical Trials Laboratory (Boston, MA, USA). Galectin‐3 was measured at randomization using the Alinity (Abbott Diagnostics) assay. This assay's limit of quantitation is 4.0 ng/mL, with a limit of blank and limit of detection of 1.0 and 1.1 ng/mL, respectively. The coefficient of variation during daily quality control testing was 4.1% at 10 ng/mL and 4.4% at both 21 and 76 ng/mL. The primary outcome of the present analyses was a centrally adjudicated kidney‐specific composite endpoint (Kidney‐EP), including the components of a sustained decrease of ≥40% in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration equation including race in the equation) to <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 , new end‐stage kidney disease or kidney‐related death. The risk of the kidney‐EP was compared between patients stratified by quartiles of baseline galectin‐3, using the lowest quartile as the referent group. Cox models were adjusted for age, sex, race, body mass index (BMI), hypertension, diabetes duration, established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), history of heart failure, baseline eGFR, high‐sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hsTnT), N‐terminal pro‐b‐type natriuretic peptide (NT‐proBNP) and urine albumin‐creatinine ratio (uACR). Change in galectin‐3 from baseline (randomization) to 6 months was compared between patients randomized to dapagliflozin and placebo using the ratio of geometric means. Results Of 17 160 patients randomized in DECLARE‐TIMI 58, galectin‐3 was available in 14,530 (84.7%) with a median 14.0 ng/mL (Q1: ≤11.9, Q4: ≥18.4) at baseline. Higher galectin‐3 quartile (Q4 vs. Q1) was associated with older age [65 (25th, 75th percentile: 61, 70) vs. 62 (58, 67) years, P trend <0.001], more frequent history of heart failure (12.2% vs. 9.4%, P < 0.001), and a longer duration of T2DM [11 (7, 17) vs. 10 (6, 15) years, P < 0.001]. There were no clinically relevant difference in BMI [31.6 (27.7, 36.2) vs. 31.3 (28.3, 34.9) kg/m 2 P = 0.03], ASCVD (41.9% vs. 40.3%, P = 0.062), or HbA1c (8.3 ± 1.2 vs. 8.3 ± 1.2, P = 0.17). Overall, patients in the highest galectin‐3 quartile had less favourable metrics of baseline kidney function [eGFR 81 (66, 93) vs. 93 (83, 100) mL/min/1.73 m 2 , P < 0.001; uACR >300 mg/g 9.6% vs. 4.6%, P < 0.001]. In the population with available galectin‐3 concentrations at baseline, 314 composite kidney events were observed. There was a significant increasing gradient of risk for the kidney‐EP across quartiles of galectin‐3 ( Figure ). This pattern was directionally consistent for individual components of the composite endpoint: ≥40% eGFR decrease (3.27% vs. 1.06%), end‐stage renal disease (0.29% vs. 0.03%) and renal death (0.3% vs. 0.0%). Adjusting for clinical characteristics, higher galectin‐3 concentration was independently associated with higher risk for the kidney‐EP ( Figure ). The c‐statistic without galectin‐3 was 0.72 and with galectin‐3 was 0.73. Figure 1 (A) Adjusted relative hazard of the kidney‐specific outcome stratified by quartiles of galectin‐3. The covariates used for adjustment are provided in the methods section. To the right of the plot, the number of events and 4 year Kaplan–Meier event rates are shown for each component of the composite endpoint. (B) Kaplan–Meier event rates are shown for each treatment group stratified by baseline galectin‐3 quartiles. The HR (95% confidence interval) and absolute risk reduction (95% confidence interval) comparing dapagliflozin versus placebo are provided within each quartile of galectin‐3. ARR, absolute risk reduction; eGFR, estimated glomerular filtration rate; HR, hazard ratio; RRR, relative risk reduction. In this nested biomarker cohort, dapagliflozin significantly reduced the risk of the kidney‐EP [hazard ratio (HR) 0.45 (95% CI 0.23, 0.85), P < 0.001], consistent with its effect in the overall trial population. This relative benefit was consistent across all galectin‐3 quartiles ( P < 0.001 for all quartiles, P interaction = 0.97; Figure ). Additionally, the absolute risk reduction achieved with dapagliflozin increased across galectin‐3 quartiles ( P trend = 0.048). From baseline to 6 months, dapagliflozin did not affect galectin‐3 concentration in subsets of patients randomized to dapagliflozin ( n = 264) or placebo [ n = 248; ratio of geometric means (95% CI) 1.01 (0.97, 1.06) P = 0.60]. Discussion In this nested biomarker study, galectin‐3 was independently associated with kidney function and its decline in patients with T2DM without CKD. Notably, galectin‐3 concentrations identified patients at higher absolute risk for kidney function decline and who derived a greater absolute benefit when treated with dapagliflozin. Improved assessment of the risk of developing future CKD in T2DM is clinically desirable. While eGFR and uACR describe current kidney function, galectin‐3 has the potential to refine risk assessment with respect to future kidney function. In this analysis, galectin‐3 was significantly associated with future decline in kidney function after accounting for eGFR and uACR. Importantly, the benefit of dapagliflozin with respect to a reduction in the kidney‐EP was consistent irrespective of baseline galectin‐3 levels. However, the significant trend towards greater absolute risk reduction in those with higher galectin‐3 levels highlights the potential to identify patients who may achieve the most pronounced benefit from therapy at an early disease phase when conventional measures of kidney function are still considered normal. The specificity of galectin‐3 as a biomarker for kidney function decline warrants further investigation. While galectin‐3 is implicated in acute kidney injury and kidney fibrosis and might serve as a target for antifibrotic therapies as shown in preclinical studies, , other studies have described its relevance to fibrotic processes in other organs as well (e.g., the heart). , Importantly, in preclinical models, pharmacological targeting resulted in reduced galectin‐3 and fibrosis and better function in both kidney and heart. , Moreover, galectin‐3 is associated with a higher incidence of heart failure, with involvement in myocardial fibrosis as a response to myocardial damage. , , Thus, galectin‐3 may play a role in the interconnected relationship between CKD and heart failure. On the other hand, this complex interplay challenges the attribution of galectin‐3 to a single pathological pathway. Given its involvement in fibrotic processes across multiple organs, galectin‐3 might be considered as a general marker of risk that reflects the sum of multiple disease processes. In the context of heart–kidney disease, galectin‐3 could be upregulated due to cardiac pathology being the main driver, but could also be elevated due to subclinical or clinical progression of the cardio‐renal syndrome with or without kidney fibrosis. In patients with diabetes, who are particularly vulnerable to both cardiac and renal complications, it becomes particularly difficult to disentangle whether elevated galectin‐3 concentrations primarily reflect a specific cardiac or kidney pathology or both. Galectin‐3 was not affected by treatment with dapagliflozin over the course of 6 months, suggesting that the observed benefits are not directly mediated by galectin‐3. However, galectin‐3 is considered a marker of fibrosis, a process that develops over a longer time span, and therefore, long‐term changes in galectin‐3 may offer additional insights into the interplay with worsening kidney function. Conclusions Plasma Gal‐3 is independently associated with the progression of kidney dysfunction in patients with T2DM and normal kidney function. The relative treatment effect of dapagliflozin was similar across galectin‐3 concentrations, with a larger absolute risk reduction observed in patients with higher galectin‐3 concentrations due to their higher baseline risk. Further studies need to clarify if the application of galectin‐3 improves risk stratification.
